newsitem.title: USA: U.S. firm Becton in China, India ventures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firm Becton in China, India ventures.

text.p: U.S. medical devices and diagnostic products maker Becton, Dickinson and Co said Friday it was comfortable with fiscal 1997 earnings estimates of around $2.40 per share, fuelled by a focus on top-line growth.

In an interview with Reuters, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Clateo Castellini said: "We'd like to grow the top line between seven and eight percent by the end of 1997. In the last three years, we had five to six percent underlying growth, but now we'd like to grow a bit faster."
The First Call mean 1997 earnings estimate was $2.43 per share. In fiscal 1996, ended September 30, it earned $2.11 per share.
In the recently reported fourth quarter, Becton Dickinson, which celebrates its centennial this year, reported top line growth which was close to nine percent, he said.
"That pace a bit high for the entire year but it is a good start," Castellini said. The only caveat to the forecast was a strong dollar, he said.

To achieve this growth, Castellini said the company had reorganized more clearly around its seven different worldwide lines of business, while expanding geographically and keeping an eye on research and development.

"Each of the seven businesses is led by a manager who acts as the CEO of that business and reports directly to me," Castellini said. "The manager always must think of growing that business and making it profitable."
Before, operational presidents reported to a layer of sector presidents who in turn reported to Castellini, he said.
The seven core areas are diabetes health care, infusion therapy, injection systems, flow cytometry, infectious disease diagnostics, sample collection and tissue culture, he said.

"We are in a particularly good position for drug delivery systems and are thinking about care moving from the hospitals into the homes," Castellini said. "We are looking into home therapy with special products."
Injection systems, the umbrella title for drug delivery products, generated between $800 million and $900 million worldwide in annual revenues for Becton, he said.

Diabetes health care, for insulin injection systems and diabetes education, had annual global sales of about $400 million, while sample collection, focused on evacuated blood collection systems, had annual sales of between $400 million and $500 million, he said.
Castellini said Becton is trying to expand its diabetes line, and also produce safer versions of its so-called "sharps" line of products, or needles and blades.
"This is a big thrust in the United States," he said.
Geographic expansion and more focused research and development spending are other growth engines for the company, Castellini said.
"We are expanding into new markets," he said. "We have a new plant in China and are starting to build one in India."
Castellini said Becton Dickinson had free cash flow after capital investments and dividends of about $400 million, which it could use to fund acquisitions and partnerships.
"But we are not after major acquisitions and have no need to buy just to get bigger," he said.
Premiums are high on many potential acquisitions targets, making buyouts financially tough to justify, he said.
Becton generally sought to buy smaller companies for under $100 million which were a good strategic fit.
"We looked at several acquisitions, some larger than $100 million, but they were just too expensive," he said.
"We don't think it will happen but this is the only red flag we raise to analysts," he said. "The movement of the dollar is always somewhat unpredictable."
Castellini said roughly half of Becton Dickinson's revenues come from outside the United States.
